subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 149(1) - Woman Director Mandate
question: Aman Steels Ltd., an unlisted public company, has a paid-up share capital of ₹80 Crores and an annual turnover of ₹320 Crores as per its latest audited financial statements for FY 2023-24. On June 15, 2024, the sole woman director resigned due to personal reasons. What is the statutory time limit by which the company must fill the intermittent vacancy under Section 149(1) read with Rule 3 of the Companies (Appointment and Qualification of Directors) Rules, 2014?
options: At the earliest but not later than immediate next Board meeting or 3 months from the date of vacancy, whichever is later.
Within 30 days from the date of resignation submitted by the woman director.
Within 6 months from the date of vacancy as per the General Circular of MCA.
At the immediate next Annual General Meeting (AGM) of the company.
ref: Section 149(1) second proviso read with Rule 3 of Companies (Appointment & Qualification of Directors) Rules, 2014
explanation: Under the second proviso to Section 149(1) and Rule 3, every listed company and every unlisted public company having paid-up share capital ≥ ₹100 Crore OR turnover ≥ ₹300 Crore must have at least one woman director. Since turnover is ₹320 Cr, the rule applies. Any intermittent vacancy must be filled by the Board at the earliest but not later than immediate next Board meeting or 3 months from the date of such vacancy, whichever is later.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 149(4) & 149(6) - Independent Director Qualification & Tenure
question: Mr. Rajan was appointed as an Independent Director of Trident Pharma Ltd. for a term of 5 consecutive years commencing April 1, 2019. In July 2023, his son was appointed as a Chief Financial Officer (CFO) in a subsidiary company of Trident Pharma Ltd. Trident Pharma Ltd. now proposes to re-appoint Mr. Rajan for a second consecutive term of 5 years with effect from April 1, 2024. Which of the following statements is legally correct under Section 149(6)?
options: Mr. Rajan is disqualified from being appointed as an Independent Director because his relative (son) holds the position of a Key Managerial Personnel (CFO) in a subsidiary company during the preceding three financial years.
Mr. Rajan can be re-appointed by passing an Ordinary Resolution in general meeting without any impediment since the son is in a subsidiary, not the holding company.
Mr. Rajan can only be appointed if approval from the Central Government (Ministry of Corporate Affairs) is obtained prior to general meeting.
The restriction on relatives being KMP applies only to spouse and parents, not sons or daughters under the definition of relative in Section 2(77).
ref: Section 149(6)(e)(i) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 149(6)(e)(i), a person is not eligible to be an Independent Director if none of his relatives holds or has held the position of a Key Managerial Personnel (KMP) or is or has been employee of the company or its holding, subsidiary or associate company in any of the three financial years immediately preceding the financial year in which he is proposed to be appointed. Since the son is a KMP (CFO) in a subsidiary, Mr. Rajan ceases to meet the independence criteria.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 164(2) - Disqualification of Directors for Company Default
question: Apex Motors Ltd. failed to file its financial statements and annual returns for three continuous financial years (FY 2020-21, 2021-22, and 2022-23) with the Registrar of Companies. Mr. Vikram was appointed as an additional director on the Board of Apex Motors Ltd. on December 1, 2023. On January 10, 2024, another company, Zenith Infotech Ltd., where Mr. Vikram was already a director, intends to re-appoint him at its AGM. Under Section 164(2) proviso, what is the status of Mr. Vikram's disqualification?
options: Mr. Vikram shall not incur disqualification under Section 164(2) in Zenith Infotech Ltd. for a period of six months from the date of his appointment in Apex Motors Ltd.
Mr. Vikram incurs immediate automatic disqualification under Section 164(2) for 5 years across all companies from the moment he joined Apex Motors Ltd.
Mr. Vikram is disqualified for lifetime from being appointed as director in any public company unless compounded by NCLT.
Disqualification under Section 164(2) applies only to Managing Directors and Whole-Time Directors, exempting Additional Directors.
ref: Section 164(2) proviso (inserted by Companies (Amendment) Act, 2017)
explanation: Under the proviso to Section 164(2), where a person is appointed as a director of a company which is in default of clause (a) or clause (b) of subsection (2), he shall not incur the disqualification for a period of six months from the date of his appointment. This provides a 6-month grace period for newly appointed directors to rectify defaults.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 165 - Maximum Number of Directorships
question: Ms. Shalini currently holds directorships in 18 companies, comprising 8 public companies and 10 private companies. Two of the private companies are dormant companies under Section 455, and one is a Section 8 non-profit company. She is now offered an alternate directorship in an unlisted public company. Can Ms. Shalini accept this new directorship without violating Section 165?
options: Yes, because dormant companies and Section 8 companies are excluded from the ceiling of 20 total companies and 10 public companies under Section 165, and alternate directorship is counted towards the ceiling.
No, because alternate directorships cannot be counted under any circumstances under the Companies Act, 2013.
No, because a person can never hold directorship in more than 10 companies of any class under the revised MCA norms.
Yes, but only if prior approval of the Central Government is obtained through Form DIR-12.
ref: Section 165(1) read with Explanation I & II of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 165(1), the maximum number of directorships is 20, of which public companies cannot exceed 10. Directorship in a dormant company (Sec 455) and Section 8 company are excluded from the limit. Alternate directorship is explicitly included in calculating limits. Here: Active public companies = 8 (+1 proposed = 9 ≤ 10); Active total = 8 public + 8 active private = 16 (+1 = 17 ≤ 20). Hence, she can legally accept.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 173 - Board Meetings & Quorum for Interested Directors
question: The Board of Directors of Pioneer Infrastructure Ltd. consists of 9 directors. At a meeting convened to consider a commercial contract involving an entity in which 7 directors are interested under Section 184(2), only 2 non-interested directors are present in person. What constitutes a valid quorum for transacting this specific business under Section 174(3)?
options: The quorum shall be the number of non-interested directors who are present at the meeting being not less than two.
A minimum of one-third of the total strength (i.e., 3 directors) is mandatory; hence the meeting must be adjourned for want of quorum.
All 7 interested directors can vote after making an oral disclosure of interest in the meeting.
The contract must be referred directly to the Central Government since quorum cannot be formed.
ref: Section 174(3) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 174(3), where at any time the number of interested directors exceeds or is equal to two-thirds of the total strength of the Board, the number of directors who are not interested and present at the meeting, being not less than two, shall be the quorum during such time for that business. Here 7 out of 9 are interested (≥ 2/3rd = 6); the 2 disinterested directors present constitute valid quorum.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 177 - Audit Committee Mandatory Constitution & Functions
question: Kiran Fabricators Ltd., an unlisted public company, has paid-up share capital of ₹8 Crores, turnover of ₹85 Crores, and outstanding bank borrowings and debentures aggregating ₹120 Crores. Is the company required to constitute an Audit Committee under Section 177 read with Rule 4 of Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014?
options: Yes, because its outstanding loans, borrowings, debentures or deposits exceed ₹50 Crores.
No, because paid-up capital is below ₹10 Crores and turnover is below ₹100 Crores.
No, constitution of Audit Committee is mandatory only for equity-listed public companies.
Yes, but only if at least 100 members requisition the Board in writing.
ref: Section 177(1) read with Rule 4 of Companies (Meetings of Board & Powers) Rules, 2014
explanation: Under Rule 4, the Board of every unlisted public company having: (a) paid-up capital ≥ ₹10 Cr; OR (b) turnover ≥ ₹100 Cr; OR (c) outstanding loans, debentures, deposits > ₹50 Cr, must constitute an Audit Committee. Since borrowings/debentures are ₹120 Cr (> ₹50 Cr), constitution of Audit Committee is mandatory.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 185 - Loans to Directors & Controlled Entities
question: Solaris Power Ltd. desires to advance a loan of ₹15 Crores to Helios Green Energy Pvt. Ltd. Mr. Arvind is a director of Solaris Power Ltd. and holds 28% of the total voting power in Helios Green Energy Pvt. Ltd. Under the amended Section 185, under what conditions can Solaris Power Ltd. advance this loan?
options: A special resolution must be passed in general meeting with explanatory statement disclosing full particulars, and the borrowing company must utilise the loan exclusively for its principal business activities.
The loan is completely prohibited under Section 185(1) as loans to any entity where a director holds >20% voting power cannot be given under any circumstances.
Only an ordinary resolution in Board meeting is required with the consent of all directors present.
The loan can be given only with prior approval of NCLT and Reserve Bank of India.
ref: Section 185(2) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 185(2), a company may advance any loan or give guarantee/security to any person in whom any of the directors is interested (which includes a private company where a director holds ≥25% voting power) provided: (a) a special resolution is passed in general meeting; and (b) the loans are utilised by the borrowing company for its principal business activities.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 186 - Loans & Investments by Company
question: Blue Horizon Ltd. has paid-up share capital of ₹50 Crores, free reserves of ₹30 Crores, and securities premium account of ₹20 Crores. The Board of Directors wishes to grant a loan of ₹65 Crores to a business partner firm. What is the statutory requirement under Section 186(3) for giving this loan?
options: Prior approval by Special Resolution in general meeting is mandatory, because the aggregate loan exceeds 60% of paid-up capital, free reserves & securities premium (60% of ₹100 Cr = ₹60 Cr) and 100% of free reserves & securities premium (₹50 Cr).
Only unanimous Board resolution is sufficient as the amount is less than 100% of paid-up capital.
Ordinary resolution in AGM is sufficient with prior sanction of ROC.
No resolution is needed if the rate of interest is higher than the bank rate.
ref: Section 186(2) and 186(3) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 186(2), a company cannot directly or indirectly give loan/guarantee/security exceeding 60% of (Paid-up capital + Free reserves + Securities premium) OR 100% of (Free reserves + Securities premium), whichever is more, without prior approval by special resolution. Here: 60% of ₹100 Cr = ₹60 Cr; 100% of ₹50 Cr = ₹50 Cr. Threshold = ₹60 Cr. Since proposed loan is ₹65 Cr (> ₹60 Cr), prior Special Resolution is required.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 188 - Related Party Transactions & Threshold Limits
question: Sigma Electronics Ltd., a public company, proposes to enter into a contract for sale of manufactured goods amounting to ₹120 Crores to Delta Components Pvt. Ltd., an entity where the Managing Director of Sigma holds 30% shares. The annual turnover of Sigma Electronics Ltd. as per its latest audited balance sheet is ₹900 Crores. Does this transaction require prior approval by Ordinary Resolution under Section 188 read with Rule 15?
options: Yes, because the contract value of ₹120 Crores exceeds 10% of the annual turnover of the company (10% of ₹900 Cr = ₹90 Cr).
No, approval of shareholders is needed only if contract value exceeds ₹100 Crores regardless of turnover.
No, only Audit Committee approval is needed; shareholder resolution is never required for sale of goods.
Yes, but it requires a Special Resolution passed with 75% majority, not an Ordinary Resolution.
ref: Section 188(1) read with Rule 15(3) of Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014
explanation: Under Rule 15(3)(a)(i), contracts or arrangements with respect to sale, purchase or supply of any goods or materials directly or through appointment of agent exceeding 10% of turnover requires prior approval of the company by ordinary resolution. 10% of ₹900 Cr = ₹90 Cr. Since ₹120 Cr > ₹90 Cr, prior ordinary resolution in general meeting is required.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 197 & Schedule V - Managerial Remuneration Limits
question: Quantum Infotech Ltd., a public company with 3 whole-time directors and 1 managing director, has earned a net profit of ₹40 Crores computed under Section 198 for FY 2023-24. What is the maximum managerial remuneration payable to all managerial personnel without seeking approval of the Central Government?
options: 10% of net profits (₹4.0 Crores) if there is more than one such director, and overall 11% of net profits (₹4.4 Crores) for all directors including non-executive directors.
5% of net profits regardless of the number of whole-time directors.
15% of net profits provided unanimous consent of the Board of Directors is obtained.
Unlimited remuneration provided an ordinary resolution is passed in the Annual General Meeting.
ref: Section 197(1) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 197(1), total managerial remuneration payable by a public company to its directors shall not exceed 11% of net profits. Remuneration payable to any one managing director or whole-time director shall not exceed 5% of net profits, and if there is more than one such director, remuneration shall not exceed 10% of net profits to all of them together. Beyond 11%, a special resolution is required.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 203 - Mandatory Appointment of KMP
question: Zenith Retail Pvt. Ltd. has a paid-up share capital of ₹12 Crores and turnover of ₹80 Crores. Is Zenith Retail Pvt. Ltd. mandatorily required to appoint a whole-time Company Secretary under Section 203 read with Rule 8A of Companies (Appointment and Remuneration of Managerial Personnel) Rules, 2014?
options: Yes, because every private company having a paid-up share capital of ₹10 Crores or more is required to appoint a whole-time Company Secretary.
No, mandatory appointment of KMP applies exclusively to listed public companies.
No, the threshold for private companies was raised to ₹50 Crores in the recent MCA amendment.
Yes, but only if the company has more than 200 employees on its payroll.
ref: Rule 8A of Companies (Appointment and Remuneration of Managerial Personnel) Rules, 2014
explanation: Under Rule 8A (as amended w.e.f. April 1, 2020), every private company which has a paid-up share capital of ₹10 Crores or more shall have a whole-time company secretary. Since Zenith Retail Pvt. Ltd. has paid-up share capital of ₹12 Crores (≥ ₹10 Cr), it must appoint a whole-time CS.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 101 & 103 - Notice of General Meeting & Quorum
question: A public company having 4,500 members convenes an Extraordinary General Meeting (EGM). At the appointed time, only 12 members are personally present. After waiting for 30 minutes, 14 members are personally present. What is the legal consequence regarding quorum under Section 103?
options: The meeting stands adjourned to the same day in the next week at the same time and place, because the required quorum for a company having between 1,000 and 5,000 members is 15 members personally present.
The 14 members present constitute valid quorum since the shortfall is less than 10%.
The meeting is immediately dissolved as an EGM cannot be adjourned under any circumstances.
The Chairman can use his casting vote to declare quorum validly established.
ref: Section 103(1)(a) and 103(2) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 103(1)(a), for a public company: (i) 5 members personally present if members ≤ 1,000; (ii) 15 members if members > 1,000 but ≤ 5,000; (iii) 30 members if members > 5,000. Here members = 4,500, so quorum is 15 members personally present. Since only 14 were present within 30 minutes, the meeting stands adjourned to next week unless called by requisitionists.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 135 - Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) Expenditure
question: Avon Chemicals Ltd. had an unspent CSR amount of ₹45 Lakhs relating to an 'ongoing project' for FY 2023-24. By what date must this unspent amount be transferred to a special account, and within what period must it be spent under Section 135(6)?
options: Transferred to 'Unspent CSR Account' in a scheduled bank within 30 days from the end of the financial year, and spent within 3 financial years from the date of transfer.
Transferred to a Fund specified in Schedule VII within 6 months from the end of the financial year.
Carried forward in general reserves indefinitely with approval of the Board of Directors.
Refunded to the Ministry of Corporate Affairs within 90 days from the Annual General Meeting.
ref: Section 135(6) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 135(6), any unspent CSR amount pursuant to any ongoing project shall be transferred by the company within 30 days from the end of the financial year to a special account titled 'Unspent Corporate Social Responsibility Account', and such amount shall be spent within a period of 3 financial years from the date of such transfer, failing which it must be transferred to a Schedule VII fund within 30 days from completion of the third financial year.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 168 - Resignation of Director & Effective Date
question: Dr. Nair, an independent director of Bharat Biotech Ltd., tendered his resignation via a written notice dated October 5, specifying that the resignation shall take effect from November 1. The company received the notice on October 8, and the Board noted the resignation on October 20. Under Section 168(2), what is the effective date of Dr. Nair's resignation?
options: November 1, because the resignation takes effect from the date specified in the notice since it is later than the date of receipt.
October 5, the date on which the letter was drafted and signed.
October 8, the date on which the company received the notice.
October 20, the date on which the Board took formal record of the resignation.
ref: Section 168(2) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 168(2), the resignation of a director shall take effect from the date on which the notice is received by the company or the date, if any, specified by the director in the notice, whichever is later. Here specified date (Nov 1) is later than receipt date (Oct 8); hence effective date is November 1.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 180 - Restrictions on Powers of Board
question: The Board of Directors of Pioneer Logistics Ltd. intends to sell an undertaking comprising a specialized fleet division whose book value is ₹42 Crores. The company's total net worth as per the audited balance sheet of the preceding financial year is ₹180 Crores. Does this sale require authorization by Special Resolution under Section 180(1)(a)?
options: Yes, because the investment in the undertaking exceeds 20% of the net worth of the company (20% of ₹180 Cr = ₹36 Cr).
No, because Board approval alone is sufficient for selling assets unless the whole company is being liquidated.
No, ordinary resolution in general meeting is sufficient under the amended rules.
Yes, but only if financial institutions have a charge registered over the undertaking.
ref: Section 180(1)(a) read with Explanation (i) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 180(1)(a), the Board can sell, lease or dispose of the whole or substantially the whole of the undertaking only with the consent of the company by special resolution. An 'undertaking' means an undertaking in which the investment of the company exceeds 20% of its net worth OR which generates 20% of total income. Here ₹42 Cr / ₹180 Cr = 23.33% (> 20%). Hence Special Resolution is mandatory.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 184 - Disclosure of Interest by Directors
question: Mr. Somani, a director of Nexus Tech Ltd., enters into a contract on behalf of Nexus Tech Ltd. with a partnership firm in which his wife holds a 60% share. Mr. Somani does not disclose his interest at the Board meeting where the contract is discussed and voted on. What are the legal consequences under Section 184(4) and Section 184(3)?
options: The contract shall be voidable at the option of Nexus Tech Ltd., and Mr. Somani shall be punishable with fine which may extend to ₹1,00,000, and shall vacate office under Section 167(1)(c).
The contract is valid and binding provided it is executed at fair arm's length market price.
Mr. Somani is solely subjected to a reprimand by the Chairman without any statutory penalty.
The firm must be compulsorily converted into a private limited company within 3 months.
ref: Section 184(3) and 184(4) read with Section 167(1)(c) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 184(3), a contract entered into by the company without disclosure of interest under subsection (2) shall be voidable at the option of the company. Under Section 184(4), non-compliance attracts fine up to ₹1,00,000. Under Section 167(1)(c), the director shall vacate his office if he fails to disclose his interest.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 110 - Passing of Resolutions by Postal Ballot
question: Greenfield Agro Ltd., an unlisted public company with 800 members, wishes to pass an ordinary resolution for the alteration of the objects clause of its Memorandum of Association. Which of the following modes is legally mandated or permissible under Section 110 read with Rule 22?
options: Alteration of objects clause for which money was raised from public through prospectus requires passing resolution only by postal ballot, but companies having members up to 200 are exempt from postal ballot rules.
Postal ballot is optional and the resolution can only be transacted at an Annual General Meeting.
Postal ballot can never be used for changing the objects clause under the Companies Act, 2013.
Postal ballot requires physical ballot papers only; electronic voting is prohibited for alteration of objects.
ref: Section 110(1) read with Rule 22 of Companies (Management & Administration) Rules, 2014
explanation: Under Section 110(1) read with Rule 22(16), alteration of objects clause of MOA is an item of business which must be transacted only by means of postal ballot (which includes electronic voting). However, One Person Companies and companies having members up to 200 are not required to transact any business through postal ballot.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 161(2) - Appointment of Alternate Director
question: Mr. Adams, a non-executive director of Horizon Global Ltd., goes abroad for a continuous period of 5 months. The Board appoints Mr. Verma as an alternate director. Mr. Verma is already an alternate director for another director in the same company. Can Mr. Verma act as an alternate director for Mr. Adams under Section 161(2)?
options: No, because a person cannot be appointed as an alternate director for more than one director in the same company, nor if he holds any directorship in the same company.
Yes, a person can hold up to three alternate directorships in the same company.
Yes, provided approval of shareholders by special resolution is obtained within 30 days.
No, because an alternate director can only be appointed if the original director is absent for at least 12 months.
ref: Section 161(2) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 161(2), the Board of Directors of a company may appoint a person, not being a person holding any alternate directorship for any other director in the company or holding directorship in the same company, to act as an alternate director for a director during his absence for a period of not less than 3 months from India. Hence, Mr. Verma cannot be appointed.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 167 - Vacation of Office of Director
question: Mr. Kapoor, director of Sterling Castings Ltd., fails to attend any Board meetings held during a period of 12 continuous months, even though leave of absence was granted to him for all meetings. Under Section 167(1)(b), what is the legal position of Mr. Kapoor's directorship?
options: His office as director becomes vacant automatically from the date of the meeting held immediately after the expiry of 12 months, regardless of whether leave of absence was granted or not.
His office remains intact because leave of absence was formally granted by the Board.
Vacation takes effect only after the company sends a 30-day show cause notice to Mr. Kapoor.
Vacation applies only if he misses 6 consecutive general meetings of shareholders.
ref: Section 167(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013
explanation: Under Section 167(1)(b), the office of a director shall become vacant in case he absents himself from all the meetings of the Board of Directors held during a period of twelve months with or without seeking leave of absence of the Board. Thus, obtaining leave of absence does not protect a director if he is absent for 12 continuous months.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 178 - Nomination and Remuneration Committee (NRC)
question: Starlight Textiles Ltd., an unlisted public company, has paid-up share capital of ₹15 Crores, turnover of ₹80 Crores, and bank loans of ₹40 Crores. Does Starlight Textiles Ltd. require the constitution of a Nomination and Remuneration Committee under Section 178(1) read with Rule 6?
options: Yes, because its paid-up share capital exceeds ₹10 Crores.
No, because its turnover is below ₹100 Crores and borrowings are below ₹50 Crores.
No, NRC is required only for listed entities with market capitalization > ₹1,000 Crores.
Yes, but only if it employs more than 500 contract workers.
ref: Section 178(1) read with Rule 6 of Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014
explanation: Under Section 178(1) read with Rule 6, every listed public company and unlisted public companies having: (a) paid-up capital ≥ ₹10 Cr; OR (b) turnover ≥ ₹100 Cr; OR (c) outstanding loans/debentures/deposits > ₹50 Cr, must constitute a Nomination and Remuneration Committee. Since paid-up capital is ₹15 Cr (≥ ₹10 Cr), NRC is mandatory.
